title: Section 114 — the councils that went bust
hook: In the 20 years before 2018, one English council issued a Section 114 notice. In the six years since, there have been at least nine.
lede: A Section 114 notice is the closest a UK council gets to declaring bankruptcy — the statutory signal from a chief finance officer that the authority cannot balance its books. Between 2000 and 2017 it was issued once, in Hackney. Since 2018 it has been issued at Northamptonshire, Croydon (three times), Slough, Thurrock, Woking, Birmingham, Nottingham and Havering.
body_md:
**Northamptonshire (February 2018 and July 2018)** was the canary. Years of Conservative-led 'Next Generation Council' transformation had left a £65m in-year gap. Commissioners arrived; the county was abolished; two new unitaries (North and West Northamptonshire) launched in 2021. The cause was judged to be chronic under-funding mixed with aggressive transformation — a pattern that would repeat.

**Croydon (2020, 2022, twice-more-in-2023)** is the textbook fiasco. A local-authority-owned company, Brick by Brick, borrowed hundreds of millions to develop housing; a hotel purchase (Croydon Park) went sour; and a £65m/year pre-existing structural deficit compounded. Commissioners arrived in October 2020; the Mayor of Croydon role was created by local referendum. Cumulative borrowing to write off: roughly £1.6bn.

**Slough (July 2021)** revealed £100m of unusable accounts — the council had capitalised revenue expenditure for years. Commissioners, asset sales, and a rebasing of the general fund followed.

**Thurrock (December 2022)** was a unique case: a unitary council in Essex that invested £1.5bn in solar farms and bond portfolios via treasury management, backed by PWLB borrowing, in a strategy reminiscent of a hedge fund. The investments soured; commissioners arrived; £452m was written off in 2023-24 alone.

**Woking (June 2023)** was Thurrock with property: £1.9bn of PWLB borrowing funnelled into the Victoria Square hotel-and-apartment development, the Sheerwater regeneration, and a failed skyscraper. For a borough of 104,000 residents, £18,000 of borrowing per head. Commissioners ordered a ten-year asset-disposal plan.

**Birmingham (September 2023)** was not investment failure — it was the unfunded liability from 170,000 female workers' equal-pay claims, estimated at £760m and rising, plus a disastrous Oracle ERP implementation costing £216m against a £19m original budget. Europe's largest local authority entered commissioner-led restructuring including Museums disposal and a 21% Council Tax rise across two years.

**Nottingham (November 2023)** was partly Robin Hood Energy — the council-owned energy supplier that lost £38m before liquidation in 2020 — and partly sustained pressure on adult social care and children's services. General-fund reserves had been exhausted.

**Havering (2025)** and several others are running on exceptional financial support — Treasury-permitted capitalisation directions that allow councils to fund revenue deficits from capital receipts or extra borrowing — at scale. MHCLG's 2024-25 settlement granted EFS to 19 councils totalling £1.35bn, a record. A further tier of 'at-risk' councils is widely reported: Hampshire, Somerset, Cheshire East, Bradford, Windsor & Maidenhead.

**The common diagnosis** from the Institute for Fiscal Studies, IfG and LGA: a 27% real-terms cut to council core spending 2010-2020, statutory-services growth (adult and children's social care, SEND transport) outstripping council tax, and a risk-taking culture that filled the gap with commercial property, treasury speculation and corporate subsidiary structures. The Fair Funding Review, delayed since 2017, is now promised for the 2026-27 local government finance settlement.
